column1: # player-copy-punctuation-allow.tsv — the em-dashes in player copy that STAY, one per row.
# Read by `scripts/check-player-copy-punctuation.py`. Three TAB-separated fields:
#     path <TAB> the exact text, with \n \t \r \\ escaped <TAB> why it keeps its dash
# ⚑ KEYED BY THE TEXT, NOT THE LINE. Lanes move lines all day; a line-number key rots into a
#   blanket ignore inside a day. Keying on the text also gives the ratchet its second edge: a row
#   whose text is no longer at that path FAILS the gate. Fixing a string RETIRES its exemption
#   instead of leaving a permission slip behind for the next dash to walk through.
# ⚑ A ROW IS AN ARGUMENT, NOT A MUTE. The reason field is required and the gate refuses an empty
#   one. "operator output", "test fixture" and "a bare — table cell" are NOT reasons to write here:
#   those are rules R3, R2 and R4 in the checker itself, and if a site of that kind is being
#   reported, the RULE is wrong and should be fixed. What belongs here is the site where the dash
#   is doing a job no punctuation rule covers.
# As of 2026-07-26 there are 19 rows in four blocks. The first three kinds are genuine
# keeps; the fourth is DEBT and says so in every row.
#   * CLAIMED-REAL OUTPUT — a page captions a <pre> block "Real output". Editing a character
#     inside it makes it not-real, which is a worse defect than the dash. Three lines.
#   * A CUTTING WORD — a haiku's kireji. It is not punctuation; removing it changes the verse.
#   * A LABELLED no-value cell — R4 catches the bare `—`, and deliberately does not try to catch
#     `<label>: —`. Widening R4 to "ends in a dash" would swallow the kireji, and widening it to
#     "ends in a dash after a colon" would be a rule written for exactly one site. One row is the
#     honest form; if a second one ever appears, THAT is the moment R4 earns the case.
